Course Standard Instrument responsibly, preserve context, control cardinality and cost, validate every telemetry

About This Part
Volume 11D adds request-level causality and code-level performance evidence to the metrics and logging platform
built in Parts A-C. It begins with trace structure and context propagation, standardizes instrumentation through
OpenTelemetry, engineers resilient Collector pipelines, controls sampling and privacy, operates Grafana Tempo, and
then integrates application performance monitoring, continuous profiling, and eBPF network visibility. The goal is not maximum telemetry volume. The goal is sufficient, trustworthy evidence to answer: which request
failed, where time was spent, what dependency was involved, which code path consumed resources, and whether the
network or policy layer contributed to the incident.
2026 Architecture Note Tempo 3.0 distributed deployments use a Kafka-compatible message queue between
ingestion and downstream trace-processing components. Treat queue sizing, durability, authentication, lag, and
recovery as part of the tracing platform design.

Scope, Safety, Privacy and Cost Controls

Use synthetic users, test services, disposable namespaces, and non-production telemetry backends for
laboratories.

Never place secrets, authorization headers, session identifiers, payment data, health data, or unnecessary
personal identifiers in span attributes, baggage, profile labels, or network-flow exports.

Apply attribute allowlists, redaction, hashing, or deletion before telemetry leaves the trust boundary. Baggage is
propagated in network headers and must be treated as externally visible context.

Define trace and profile ingest budgets, sampling targets, retention, tenant limits, query limits, object-storage
lifecycle, and emergency throttling procedures.

Use stable semantic conventions, bounded attributes, and controlled resource metadata.

Chapter 31: Distributed Tracing Fundamentals and Context
Propagation
Reconstructing request causality across services, queues, databases and asynchronous work
Trace Data Model
A distributed trace is a tree or graph-like record of work triggered by a transaction. Spans represent timed operations. Parent-child relationships describe nested work; links represent causal relationships that are not naturally hierarchical,
such as batch consumers or fan-in processing. A span normally contains a trace ID, span ID, parent span ID, name,
kind, start and end time, status, attributes, events, links, and resource identity. Element
Purpose
Design Rule
Trace ID
Correlates all spans for one distributed
transaction

never regenerate mid-request. Span name
Describes an operation

URLs or user values. Attributes

Context Propagation
Context propagation carries trace identity across process boundaries. HTTP, gRPC, messaging, scheduled work, and
background jobs need explicit injection and extraction through supported propagators. The default interoperable
choice is W3C Trace Context. Mixed environments may temporarily require B3 or vendor formats during migration, but
multiple propagators increase ambiguity and testing burden. Trace context and log correlation example
# Example request headers
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
tracestate: vendorname=value
# Application logs should copy trace identifiers from active context
{"level":"ERROR","trace_id":"4bf92f...","span_id":"00f067...","message":"payment timeout"}
Synchronous and Asynchronous Boundaries

HTTP and gRPC usually preserve a parent-child chain when client and server instrumentation agree on
propagation.

Message producers should inject context into message metadata. Consumers may create a child span for one
message or use links when processing batches or delayed work.

Retries should be represented as events or child spans so latency and repeated dependency load remain visible.

Fan-out creates multiple child branches. Fan-in should preserve links to all relevant upstream contexts rather than
inventing a false single parent.

Trace continuity is not proof of correctness. Validate timestamps, clocks, service identity, span kinds, errors, and
missing branches.

Interview Questions and Model Answers
Q: Why are links needed?
A: They represent causality that is not accurately modeled by one parent, especially batches, queues, retries and fan-
in. Q: What makes a good span name?
A: A stable operation name based on a route or logical action, with variable data stored only in controlled attributes. Chapter Summary

Chapter 32: OpenTelemetry Architecture, Resources and
Semantic Conventions
Building a vendor-neutral telemetry contract across languages and platforms
Core Components
OpenTelemetry separates telemetry creation from storage and analysis. APIs are used by application code and
instrumentation libraries. SDKs implement sampling, processors and export. Instrumentation libraries observe
frameworks and dependencies. OTLP transports telemetry. The Collector receives, transforms and exports signals. Backends store and query them. This separation allows platform teams to change backends without rewriting every
application. Layer

Resources describe the entity producing telemetry. The minimum reliable contract is a stable service.name plus
environment, service version, deployment or instance identity, and platform attributes that support ownership and
rollout comparison. Resource detection should enrich rather than overwrite deliberate application identity. Environment-based resource and exporter configuration

OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=deployment.environment.name=production,service.version=2026.08.1,service.namespace=commerce
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://otel-gateway.example.internal:4317
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc
Semantic Conventions
Semantic conventions standardize attribute names and operation meaning for HTTP, databases, messaging, RPC,
cloud, containers, Kubernetes and other domains. They enable reusable dashboards and queries, but conventions

evolve. Pin instrumentation versions, record convention stability, test migrations, and avoid creating organization-
specific aliases for fields already covered by the standard. Contract Area

default. Messaging

semantics. Errors

outcomes as failures. Schema evolution

Q: Why are semantic conventions valuable?
A: They make telemetry portable and reusable by standardizing names and meanings across languages and tools. Q: What is the difference between resource and span attributes?

Python manual span example
from opentelemetry import trace
tracer = trace.get_tracer("commerce.checkout", "1.0.0")
with tracer.start_as_current_span("checkout.validate_cart") as span:
span.set_attribute("commerce.cart.item_count", len(items))
span.set_attribute("commerce.checkout.channel", channel)
validate(items)
span.add_event("cart_validated")
Manual spans should describe business operations that automatic instrumentation cannot infer. Attributes must be
bounded and reviewed. Avoid customer names, email addresses, raw order IDs, full URLs, SQL statements, request
bodies, or tokens. Prefer a controlled business category, result, tier, or feature flag. Kubernetes Operator Pattern
Illustrative Operator-managed instrumentation resource

kind: Instrumentation
metadata:
name: platform-default
namespace: commerce
spec:
exporter:

endpoint: http://otel-agent:4318
propagators: [tracecontext, baggage]
sampler:
type: parentbased_traceidratio
argument: "0.10"
---
# Workload annotation example
instrumentation.opentelemetry.io/inject-python: "platform-default
Operator injection changes workload startup. Validate init containers, injected libraries, runtime versions, musl versus
glibc requirements, startup time, memory overhead, side effects, and rollback. Use canary namespaces and
admission-webhook monitoring before broad rollout. Instrumentation Acceptance Tests

No sensitive headers, request bodies or database values are exported.



Application behavior is unchanged when exporter or Collector is unavailable. Production Readiness Checklist

Q: When should manual instrumentation be used?
A: For domain operations and business context that framework-level automatic instrumentation cannot understand.

Chapter 34: OpenTelemetry Collector Pipelines, Topologies and
Resiliency
Operating telemetry collection as a reliable production data plane
Collector Component Model
Collector configuration defines receivers, processors, exporters, connectors and extensions. A component is inactive
until referenced by a service pipeline or extension list. Processor order is operationally significant: memory limiting
should occur early, privacy transforms before export, and batching near the end. Validate configuration with the
Collector validate command before rollout. Collector trace pipeline example
receivers:
otlp:
protocols:
grpc:
endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
http:
endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
processors:
memory_limiter:
check_interval: 1s
limit_mib: 768
spike_limit_mib: 192
attributes/privacy:
actions:
- key: http.request.header.authorization
action: delete
- key: user.email
action: delete
batch:
send_batch_size: 2048
timeout: 5s
exporters:
otlp/tempo:
endpoint: tempo-gateway.observability.svc:4317
tls:
insecure: true
sending_queue:
enabled: true
retry_on_failure:
enabled: true
extensions:
health_check:
endpoint: 0.0.0.0:13133
service:
extensions: [health_check]
pipelines:
traces:
receivers: [otlp]
processors: [memory_limiter, attributes/privacy, batch]
exporters: [otlp/tempo]

Sending queues and retry reduce loss during transient backend failure. Persistent file-backed queues can survive
Collector restart when loss is unacceptable, but require disk capacity, lifecycle monitoring and recovery tests. Queues
are not infinite storage. Define maximum outage tolerance, drop policy, alert thresholds and emergency sampling or
filtering actions.

Monitor accepted, refused, dropped and failed telemetry by signal.

Alert on exporter queue utilization, enqueue failures, retry exhaustion, memory limiter refusals, process memory,
CPU, restarts and configuration reload failures.

Tail sampling and other stateful processors cannot be scaled like stateless gateways; route all spans for a trace to
the same decision context.

Protect OTLP endpoints with TLS, authentication, network policy and bounded request size. Do not expose debug
exporters or zPages publicly.

Load test with realistic span size, burst shape, compression, tenant mix and backend outage duration.

Illustrative tail-sampling policy
processors:
tail_sampling:
decision_wait: 15s
num_traces: 50000
policies:
- name: keep-errors
type: status_code
status_code:
status_codes: [ERROR]
- name: keep-slow
type: latency
latency:
threshold_ms: 1500
- name: baseline
type: probabilistic

probabilistic:
sampling_percentage: 5
Tail sampling introduces decision delay and memory pressure. The decision wait must accommodate normal trace
completion without holding data indefinitely. Capacity must be modeled using incoming trace rate, spans per trace,
average span size, decision window and burst factor. Preserve a random baseline so healthy traffic remains
comparable. Baggage and Privacy
Baggage is propagated alongside context and may appear in network headers. It is not automatically a safe attribute
store. Use only bounded, non-secret values needed across services. Never propagate access tokens, email addresses,
customer names, raw account identifiers, authorization decisions, or regulated data. Prefer an internal opaque
category or lookup key when cross-service context is necessary. Control
Implementation
Allowlist
Only approved attribute and baggage keys may leave the service. Redaction
Delete or transform headers, query values, DB statements and
exception text before export. Sampling budget
Assign baseline and exception sampling targets per service tier. Tenant limits
Apply ingest, search, retention and concurrency limits per tenant. Audit
Sample telemetry payloads in a protected test environment and
record policy violations. Emergency mode
Pre-approved config to reduce sampling or drop low-value spans
during overload. Production Readiness Checklist

Define sampling objectives per service tier.

Preserve errors and a healthy random baseline.

Model tail-sampler memory and decision delay.

Create an attribute and baggage allowlist.

TraceQL selects traces and spans by intrinsic fields, resource attributes, span attributes, duration, status and

dependency, version or duration. Broad regular-expression queries over long periods are expensive and should be

Glossary
Term
Meaning
APM
Operational practice combining service, request, dependency,
runtime and code-level performance evidence. Baggage
Key-value contextual data propagated alongside trace context; it
requires strict privacy control. Exemplar
Reference from an aggregated metric observation to a
representative trace. OTLP
OpenTelemetry Protocol for transporting traces, metrics, logs and
supported telemetry. Resource
Attributes identifying the entity that produced telemetry. Semantic conventions
Standard attribute names and operation meanings defined by
OpenTelemetry. Span
Timed unit of work inside a trace. Tail sampling
Sampling decision made after trace data has been collected. TraceQL
Tempo query language for selecting and analyzing traces. Continuous profiling
Ongoing collection and analysis of sampled stack and runtime
resource behavior.
eBPF
Linux kernel technology used for programmable networking, security
and performance observation. Hubble
Cilium observability layer for cluster network and security flows. Official Documentation Index
